summary:
We developed WIÑAPAY (from the Quechua wiñay, meaning "to grow," "to sprout," or "to endure"), a civic and environmental web platform for Cusco that integrates NASA Earth observations with public memory and community voices. Through an interactive regional map, district dossiers comparing multi-year environmental indicators, chronological event records, consented testimonies, and a directory of local initiatives, WIÑAPAY turns scattered data into an accessible territorial tool. 
Andean wildfires and prolonged droughts are often treated as isolated map alerts or reduced to purely punitive narratives. WIÑAPAY addresses this gap by pairing open satellite indicators (vegetation vigor [MOD13Q1], land surface temperature [MOD11A2], and precipitation [GPM IMERG]) with seasonal wind context, agricultural realities, and lived local experience. Rather than stopping at passive visualization, each locality dossier explains its methodological boundaries transparently and connects users directly to vetted prevention, training, and reforestation organizations. 
Environmental crises quickly fade from headlines, leaving rural communities isolated and without lasting institutional records. WIÑAPAY preserves verifiable territorial memory across decades, bridges space science with human dignity, and empowers municipalities, youth brigades, educators, and citizens to move from reactive alarm to coordinated, long-term resilience.
details:
WHAT OUR PROJECT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

We developed WIÑAPAY ("El territorio tiene memoria. Hagamosla visible."), an interactive Progressive Web App (PWA) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge ("Be an Earth Systems Trend Detective!") that transforms NASA Earth observations into accessible, verifiable evidence of environmental change across the province of Cusco, Peru, connecting multi-decade satellite trends with real human stories. Rather than building a static map viewer, we designed a living territorial dossier structured around a four-stage user experience.

First, our landing page introduces the scope of our work (24 years of MODIS vegetation records, 2001–2025, space-detected burned-area scars, and community testimonies) offering direct entry points into either the interactive map or community stories.

Second, our awareness map displays the provincial boundary of Cusco with five pulsing hotspots placed on real burned-area scars or district centroids across different geographic zones. When a user clicks a hotspot, a symbolic water-wave animation extinguishes the red marker into gold or green and opens a modal displaying a single plain-language insight, such as vegetation loss. Once all five zones are explored, the interface automatically transitions into the analytical dashboard.

Third, our district dashboard lets users examine any district in Cusco using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI, MOD13Q1 v061 at 250 m and 16-day resolution) across mean, maximum, and dry-season aggregations, masked with burned-area data (MCD64A1) and elevation contours (NASADEM 30 m). Users select integer year ranges of at least five years through an Orbital Constellation selector, which recalculates Mann-Kendall trend tests, Sen's slope estimates, and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections directly in the browser.

Finally, our stories section links district indicators to moderated, consent-based community testimonies, investigative reports, and local territorial memory.

BENEFITS OF OUR PROJECT

Our platform demystifies complex remote-sensing data by translating statistical trend results into plain, verifiable citizen language and relatable scale metaphors. By placing orbital measurements alongside consented testimonies, we bridge scientific evidence and lived human experience so neither stands in isolation. We also engineered WIÑAPAY for full offline resilience using a custom GeoJSON-only map without external tile servers, Service Workers, and IndexedDB caching, ensuring that maps, NDVI time series, browser-based trend calculations. Additionally, users can dynamically test custom multi-year intervals between 2001 and 2025 in real time rather than relying on static reports.

INTENDED IMPACT

We created WIÑAPAY for the communities of the province of Cusco and the organizations that work alongside them, including NGOs, foundations, and corporate social programs. Our goal is to help local communities and partner organizations understand how their territory has changed over more than two decades, substantiate prevention and conservation projects with rigorous statistical evidence, report verifiable outcomes to funders, and give visibility and dignity to rural residents affected by vegetation loss and wildfires.

TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, AND SOFTWARE WE USED

On the frontend, we built our application using Next.js (App Router), React, TypeScript, Radix UI for accessible modals and dialogs, and self-hosted Google Fonts (DM Serif Display and DM Sans).

For geospatial visualization, we used MapLibre GL v5.x to render custom GeoJSON layers, including INEI district boundaries, 100 m NASADEM contour lines, and burned-area masks, without relying on an external base map. We implemented animations using GSAP and ScrollTrigger for the water-extinguishing interaction and map-to-dashboard transition, paired with pure CSS transform and opacity animations for pulsing markers.

For offline PWA capabilities, we used Serwist (Service Worker) and IndexedDB. On the backend, we used Next.js Route Handlers, Supabase (PostgreSQL with PostGIS, Auth, Row-Level Security, and Storage), and a client-side TypeScript statistical module implementing Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope, and Benjamini-Hochberg adjustments.

To process NASA Earthdata datasets (specifically MOD13Q1.061 (NDVI, EVI, and QA flags), MCD64A1.061 (burned area), NASADEM_NC.001 (elevation), and optional MCD12Q1 and MOD11A2 layers) we built a Python 3 data pipeline using pandas, xarray, scipy, and pymannkendall.

We configured continuous integration with GitHub Actions and hosting on Vercel, Netlify, or Cloudflare Pages.

HOW OUR PROJECT IS CREATIVE

Instead of confronting visitors with technical charts right away, we designed a gamified emotional discovery flow grounded in behavioral science. We calibrated the map to feature exactly five hotspots based on the Goal Gradient Effect, the Endowed Progress Effect, Miller's Law under emotional load, and scrollytelling research, using a water-wave animation to symbolically extinguish each hotspot before revealing one memorable fact.

For the analytical dashboard, we replaced traditional range sliders with a NASA-inspired Orbital Constellation period selector, where years from 2001 to 2025 appear as luminous stars (highlighted in terracotta during recorded fire years) connected by an illuminated orbital arc. We also crafted a visual identity rooted in Cusco's landscape (combining deep forest green, sage, cream, sand, terracotta, and gold) to give the platform the feel of a calm, respectful civic archive.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

We prioritized scientific rigor and epistemic honesty by focusing strictly on a single validated primary variable (NDVI with quality-assurance filtering) and discarding noisy datasets such as GPM IMERG records containing randomError. When statistical significance is not reached (p >= 0.05), our platform explicitly states that there is not yet sufficient evidence rather than claiming no change occurred, and we enforce a five-year minimum range so Mann-Kendall calculations remain valid.

We also ensured full traceability to NASA sources and required any placeholder test data to carry a visible warning banner. From an ethical standpoint, we required explicit consent for all testimonies, removed public personal identifiers, enforced pre-publication moderation, and prohibited AI-generated testimonies.

Finally, we accounted for accessibility and rural connectivity by meeting WCAG AA contrast standards, enabling full keyboard navigation, honoring reduced-motion preferences with simple fade fallbacks, adapting layouts to mobile bottom-sheets and vertical timelines, and ensuring full offline functionality.
